lines.speaker: Mei Tanaka
lines.text: Thanks for making time. This is a blameless review of Tuesday's route optimizer outage. We had 52 minutes when dispatchers could see empty routes, and I want a shared timeline before we talk about fixes.

lines.speaker: Amara Nwosu
lines.text: I appreciate that framing. Customers called support before we could explain what was happening, and I want us to separate their experience from what the backend logs happen to say.

lines.speaker: Mei Tanaka
lines.text: Agreed. We are examining the system and our response, not who happened to press deploy. Lucas, start with the change. What did we expect the new index to improve?

lines.speaker: Lucas Ferreira
lines.text: The deploy changed the index used to find stops eligible for optimizer runs. The old query had become slow on larger carrier schedules, and in staging the new plan cut that read roughly in half.

lines.speaker: Omar Haddad
lines.text: Was the index built during the outage window, or had it already been built? I ask because that changes whether we need a deployment control or a runtime control.

lines.speaker: Lucas Ferreira
lines.text: It had been built. The surprise was that a nightly job chose a different path through the tables after the index changed. It held a lock while assembling the next batch of route inputs.

lines.speaker: Mei Tanaka
lines.text: Let's pin the order down. The index deploy completed before the nightly job started. At what point did requests begin returning empty routes instead of a previous valid plan?

lines.speaker: Lucas Ferreira
lines.text: The first failed optimizer read followed the job starting its batch. The request waited on the locked table, hit our service timeout, and the caller translated that timeout into an empty route array.

lines.speaker: Jonas Weber
lines.text: That translation is important. An empty route array is a legitimate state for a carrier with nothing scheduled. The interface had no error to display, so it rendered a calm blank board.

lines.speaker: Amara Nwosu
lines.text: Right. Dispatchers were refreshing because their assignments vanished, not because they were asking for a new optimization. The first ticket says, in plain words, that every truck looked unassigned.

lines.speaker: Mei Tanaka
lines.text: Do we know when the first customer-visible empty result happened relative to our first alert? I do not want a precise timestamp here if the request logs only give us a range.

lines.speaker: Lucas Ferreira
lines.text: We can place it within two minutes from request logs. The page fired about 18 minutes after those first empty results. A support ticket arrived roughly nine minutes earlier than the page.

lines.speaker: Omar Haddad
lines.text: So the customer path was broken for close to a third of the incident before the on-call page. Please put both the first failed request and the first ticket on the timeline.

lines.speaker: Mei Tanaka
lines.text: Yes. I was on call and initially saw a normal server-health graph. The optimizer processes were alive, but that measure did not tell us whether dispatchers had usable routes.

lines.speaker: Lucas Ferreira
lines.text: The database wait graph was climbing, but it is a dashboard panel rather than a page. Once Mei opened the trace, the lock holder and the changed query plan were visible.

lines.speaker: Mei Tanaka
lines.text: I paused the nightly job first. That released the lock, but I did not declare recovery immediately because new optimizer reads still had to run and the index plan could lock again.

lines.speaker: Lucas Ferreira
lines.text: I rolled back the index change and sampled route regeneration for several affected carriers. Those requests returned populated route plans again, and we watched the next few optimizer cycles finish.

lines.speaker: Jonas Weber
lines.text: Did the empty display clear automatically once those plans returned? A dispatcher looking at the screen could have kept seeing the blank state even after the service recovered.

lines.speaker: Lucas Ferreira
lines.text: The next refresh picked up the regenerated plans. We have evidence of that in the request logs, but I do not have evidence that every open browser tab refreshed on its own.

lines.speaker: Amara Nwosu
lines.text: Support told callers to refresh after engineering confirmed the rollback. That worked for the callers we reached, but we did not have a way to identify silent users staring at a stale blank board.

lines.speaker: Mei Tanaka
lines.text: The incident window is 52 minutes from the first confirmed empty route response to stable successful optimization. It is not 52 minutes of total downtime for every one of the 31 accounts.

lines.speaker: Omar Haddad
lines.text: Thank you for saying that. I have seen the 31-customer number repeated without that distinction. We should say what the count means before it becomes a board-facing metric.

lines.speaker: Lucas Ferreira
lines.text: The recovery signal was two successful cycles across the impacted carrier set, no new empty route responses from timed-out reads, and the lock wait dropping back near baseline.

lines.speaker: Mei Tanaka
lines.text: We also left the nightly job paused after recovery. That was deliberate; a clean service graph while the job is off is not proof the underlying interaction is fixed.

lines.speaker: Amara Nwosu
lines.text: That matters for the customer note. I can say routes were restored on Tuesday, but I should not say the permanent fix shipped when we only rolled the change back.

lines.speaker: Mei Tanaka
lines.text: Exactly. Let's move from the sequence into why the safeguards did not catch the combination. Lucas, walk through the query plan and the test we did not have.

lines.speaker: Lucas Ferreira
lines.text: The new index looked right for the optimizer's frequent stop lookup. It changed the nightly job's planner choice, though, and that job scanned and updated the same route-input tables inside one long transaction.

lines.speaker: Mei Tanaka
lines.text: Did we see a table lock in staging? I remember reviewing the optimizer query time, but not a full nightly run while the new index was present.

lines.speaker: Lucas Ferreira
lines.text: No. Staging had a small schedule and a shortened nightly dataset. We tested the read query and the job separately, so neither test represented their overlap at production size.

lines.speaker: Omar Haddad
lines.text: That sounds like a predictable gap in the checklist, not a mystery. Which other changes can alter a job's plan even when the application code does not change?

lines.speaker: Lucas Ferreira
lines.text: Indexes, statistics, and batch size can all shift it. Here the index was the trigger, the nightly transaction held the lock, and our timeout-to-empty conversion made the failure look like valid data.

lines.speaker: Jonas Weber
lines.text: I want to push on that last part. If the API returned an error, the board could say routes are temporarily unavailable and retain the last known plan. Empty should mean there are truly no routes.

lines.speaker: Mei Tanaka
lines.text: Yes, but I do not want the old plan presented as current without a timestamp. A stale assignment could mislead a dispatcher into sending the wrong driver.

lines.speaker: Jonas Weber
lines.text: Fair. I can design an error panel with the last successful plan clearly labeled as earlier data, and a retry control. It cannot silently masquerade as the live board.

lines.speaker: Amara Nwosu
lines.text: Please make the words usable under stress. A dispatcher needs to know whether to wait, use an older plan, or call support. Blank space left them to guess all three.

lines.speaker: Lucas Ferreira
lines.text: On detection, I would page on database lock waits lasting more than five minutes. That is closer to the physical problem and would have fired before the server-health alert.

lines.speaker: Mei Tanaka
lines.text: I disagree with making that the primary page. Lock waits rise during planned maintenance too, while a single empty route response caused by a timeout is already a customer-visible failure.

lines.speaker: Lucas Ferreira
lines.text: A single bad response could be a harmless cancellation or a carrier with no work. If we page on every empty array, on call will drown in false positives.

lines.speaker: Jonas Weber
lines.text: Could the signal be an empty result following an optimizer timeout, rather than any empty result? The API ought to preserve that distinction so the interface and alert both know what happened.

lines.speaker: Mei Tanaka
lines.text: That is the distinction I mean. The service should report timeout as failure, and we can page when failures affect more than one carrier in a short window.

lines.speaker: Lucas Ferreira
lines.text: I can instrument a five-minute window: page on three timeout-derived route failures across two carriers, and warn on a lock wait over two minutes. We can tune with replay data.

lines.speaker: Omar Haddad
lines.text: What happens if one large carrier has a severe incident and never reaches the two-carrier rule? I do not want the threshold to hide concentration in one account.

lines.speaker: Lucas Ferreira
lines.text: Good catch. A separate page should fire after three consecutive failed route requests for one carrier. I will compare that against last month's logs to estimate noise.

lines.speaker: Mei Tanaka
lines.text: Then the customer signal is primary and lock duration helps diagnosis. We will not ship a threshold just because it looks neat on paper; the replay must show it would have caught Tuesday quickly.

lines.speaker: Amara Nwosu
lines.text: Could support see that signal too? The team opened a ticket while engineering still saw green health. Even a clear incident flag would have stopped us asking the dispatcher to clear their cache.

lines.speaker: Lucas Ferreira
lines.text: Yes. A read-only incident flag in the support view can show route generation failures without exposing internal database terms. I can add that to the alert work.

lines.speaker: Jonas Weber
lines.text: I want to test the empty-state wording against a real dispatcher before calling it done. If it says an earlier plan is available, we must show exactly when that plan was computed.

lines.speaker: Mei Tanaka
lines.text: We should also stop converting optimizer timeouts to empty arrays. That is a small code path with a large effect. I will ask the service owner to return an explicit failure and preserve the last good plan separately.

lines.speaker: Omar Haddad
lines.text: Is the nightly job safe to resume after the index rollback? Pausing it protects routes today, but leaving it paused indefinitely could create a different operational failure.

lines.speaker: Lucas Ferreira
lines.text: The old index and old plan ran together before Tuesday, but I want a bounded replay against a production-sized copy before we resume the full nightly batch. We can run a smaller slice first.

lines.speaker: Mei Tanaka
lines.text: Let's use a monitored slice and a stop condition for lock waits. I will be present for that run, and we will record the result in the incident follow-up rather than quietly flipping the job back.

lines.speaker: Amara Nwosu
lines.text: That is a good operational answer. For customers, I will call it controlled validation, not another outage or a permanent fix, unless the actual data supports stronger language.

lines.speaker: Amara Nwosu
lines.text: I reconciled support tickets with route-request logs. Thirty-one customers had at least one affected optimizer request during the incident. That does not mean all 31 lost a delivery or even opened the board.

lines.speaker: Omar Haddad
lines.text: Can we split those into customers who saw an empty board and customers whose background request failed? I need a defensible definition before we discuss credits or a public incident count.

lines.speaker: Amara Nwosu
lines.text: We can identify 31 affected accounts from failed requests, but we cannot see every human screen. Eleven contacted support, and some of those reported multiple dispatchers watching the same blank board.

lines.speaker: Jonas Weber
lines.text: That is also a design measurement gap. We log route fetches, but not whether the board rendered a blank state because of an error. A screen event could clarify real exposure next time.

lines.speaker: Lucas Ferreira
lines.text: I can join route failures to board-load events for the accounts that had active sessions. It will give a better estimate, though it still will not prove whether someone acted on an old assignment.

lines.speaker: Mei Tanaka
lines.text: Please separate confirmed experience, inferred exposure, and unknown downstream consequences in the write-up. We should be precise even if the less tidy answer takes longer to explain.

lines.speaker: Amara Nwosu
lines.text: One dispatcher said they used a printed morning route sheet while the board was blank. Another waited to release trucks. I will not turn those anecdotes into a claim about all customers.

lines.speaker: Omar Haddad
lines.text: I appreciate that. If an account asks for a credit, we can review their actual service record and contract terms. We should not preannounce a blanket remedy from a request-log count.

lines.speaker: Amara Nwosu
lines.text: The harder part is communication. Our status page stayed green until after support had eleven reports in the queue. I had no clear trigger for posting while engineering was still investigating.

lines.speaker: Mei Tanaka
lines.text: I did not hand you an incident declaration early enough. We were trying to confirm the database cause, but we already knew route creation was failing. We should have posted the symptom first.

lines.speaker: Omar Haddad
lines.text: Exactly. A status page is not a root-cause report. Customers need to know whether the service is affected now, even if the technical explanation changes during the investigation.

lines.speaker: Jonas Weber
lines.text: The label matters too. Saying all systems operational while routes are missing is worse than saying we are investigating degraded route generation. It makes the customer's own observation seem wrong.

lines.speaker: Amara Nwosu
lines.text: I want permission to publish a short investigating update when we have two independent carrier reports or a confirmed route-failure signal, without waiting for a database diagnosis.

lines.speaker: Mei Tanaka
lines.text: I am comfortable with that if the incident lead confirms the symptom. Set a ten-minute decision point: if route generation is failing, publish the status update even while we hunt the cause.

lines.speaker: Amara Nwosu
lines.text: Ten minutes from confirmed impact, with a named backup if I am on another customer call. I will draft plain language for investigating, identified, and monitoring states by tomorrow.

lines.speaker: Omar Haddad
lines.text: Who checks that those updates actually happen? We have a process on paper for other incidents, but the handoff failed here. Give me a clock and an owner in the incident log.

lines.speaker: Mei Tanaka
lines.text: The on-call incident lead owns the clock and names a communications owner at declaration. If Amara is unavailable, I will assign the backup; the declaration will not wait for the full diagnosis.

lines.speaker: Lucas Ferreira
lines.text: We should put the first customer-impact timestamp beside the status-page publish timestamp in the review. That lag is the measure we want to shrink, not just the time until we found the lock.

lines.speaker: Jonas Weber
lines.text: Could the product show a link to the status page in the route error state? It might prevent a dispatcher from hitting refresh for twenty minutes with no explanation.

lines.speaker: Amara Nwosu
lines.text: Yes, but only if the page is timely. I would rather first fix the declaration path, then link the error state to it. A green status page beside an error would repeat the contradiction.

lines.speaker: Mei Tanaka
lines.text: That order makes sense. For Tuesday, we will send a factual note to the 31 affected accounts: the 52-minute window, restored routes, and the follow-up work, without asserting a delivery outcome we cannot verify.

lines.speaker: Amara Nwosu
lines.text: I will make a separate call list for the eleven who contacted us and answer their specific questions. The broader note can acknowledge the route-generation failure and say the index change was rolled back.

lines.speaker: Omar Haddad
lines.text: Please show me the wording before it goes out, particularly any sentence about financial impact. I can review quickly today; I do not need to hold up the operational facts.

lines.speaker: Amara Nwosu
lines.text: I will send you the draft today. If we cannot verify delivery impact, the note will say so in ordinary language instead of making an assurance based only on our logs.

lines.speaker: Mei Tanaka
lines.text: Good. That gives us a communication fix and a boundary on what we know. Let's close with prevention items we can actually test and assign dates to.

lines.speaker: Mei Tanaka
lines.text: For the deploy checklist, I will add a database-change review that names every scheduled job touching the changed tables. An index deploy needs a production-sized plan check and an explicit rollback owner.

lines.speaker: Lucas Ferreira
lines.text: I can provide the optimizer query plan and the nightly job plan side by side. I will also run a bounded replay with the old index before we resume the full batch.

lines.speaker: Omar Haddad
lines.text: How do we know that checklist changed behavior rather than just adding a box? I would like one sample deploy reviewed against it, with evidence that the scheduled job was considered.

lines.speaker: Mei Tanaka
lines.text: Fair. I will publish the revised checklist by Friday and use the next database change as a review sample. The reviewer must attach both plans or explain why a job cannot touch the table.

lines.speaker: Lucas Ferreira
lines.text: I will bring the alert proposal by Friday: timeout-derived route failures across carriers, repeated failures for one carrier, and lock-wait diagnostics. The replay will show whether Tuesday would page within five minutes.

lines.speaker: Jonas Weber
lines.text: I will draft an explicit route-error state by next week. It will distinguish unavailable routes from zero routes, show the timestamp of the last good plan, and offer a safe retry.

lines.speaker: Amara Nwosu
lines.text: I will test Jonas's wording with two dispatchers once the draft is ready. I also own the status-page templates by tomorrow and the incident note for affected accounts by end of week.

lines.speaker: Mei Tanaka
lines.text: I will own the timeout-to-error service change and identify the engineer doing it today. That contract must be in place before Jonas's state can be reliable, so those tasks move together.

lines.speaker: Omar Haddad
lines.text: We should write down a completion gate: a replay under the changed index, an alert that catches the simulated failure, and a status update exercise. Otherwise each owner can finish a document while the chain still fails.

lines.speaker: Lucas Ferreira
lines.text: Agreed. I can make the replay produce a route-failure event and verify it reaches the page. I will not use the production nightly job as the first end-to-end test.

lines.speaker: Mei Tanaka
lines.text: Let's hold a short follow-up next week to review that evidence. If the replay does not reproduce the lock, we will say that honestly and keep the risky index change rolled back.

lines.speaker: Amara Nwosu
lines.text: And I will bring a timeline of the eleven customer reports against the status-page post. That should show whether our ten-minute declaration rule would have helped on Tuesday.

lines.speaker: Jonas Weber
lines.text: I will bring the board state too, including what a dispatcher sees before, during, and after a failed optimizer call. We can inspect whether the old plan label is clear.

lines.speaker: Omar Haddad
lines.text: Thank you. I am comfortable recording 31 affected customer accounts and 52 minutes of degraded route generation, with downstream delivery impact unverified. That is precise enough for the incident record.

lines.speaker: Mei Tanaka
lines.text: We have owners for the alert, checklist, error state, customer note, and communication clock. I will put these in the incident tracker today and keep the index change rolled back until the evidence review.

lines.speaker: Lucas Ferreira
lines.text: One last thing: I want the nightly job restart decision recorded separately from the index redeploy. The safe old-index slice can resume before we consider another index experiment.

lines.speaker: Mei Tanaka
lines.text: Agreed. I will make that two explicit decisions. Thanks, everyone, for being concrete and for resisting the easy story that one deploy caused everything. We will review the evidence next week.
